teaser: To finish this battle, its painter turned down the job of mayor.
review_notes:
Altdorfer declined the office of mayor of Regensburg in 1528, citing this commission from Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria.
Panel about 158 x 120 cm; said to have been trimmed on all sides, with the tablet text originally in German and later replaced by Latin.
Translation of the tablet (100,000 Persian foot soldiers and over 10,000 horsemen killed; Darius fled with about 1,000 horsemen; mother, wife and children captured).
Taken to Paris by French troops in 1800; hung in Napoleon's bathroom at Saint-Cloud; found by Prussian troops in 1814 and returned to Bavaria.
Ottoman siege of Vienna, autumn 1529; Altdorfer as city architect in charge of Regensburg's defenses.
Identification of the island as Cyprus, with the Red Sea and Nile beyond, follows the usual reading.
The image is small for the size of the figures: Darius (three white horses, about 0.30, 0.70) and Alexander (about 0.505, 0.715) were located on an enlarged crop and should be checked on a high-resolution image.

lesson.text: In 1528 Albrecht Altdorfer had everything a painter in a German town could want. He owned several houses in Regensburg, sat on the city council and held the post of city architect. That year his fellow councilors offered him the top job: mayor. He said no. He had a painting to finish.

The painting was for Duke Wilhelm IV of Bavaria, who wanted a series of famous battles from ancient history for his residence in Munich, each by a different artist. Altdorfer drew the victory of Alexander the Great over the Persian king Darius at Issus, in what is now southern Turkey, in 333 BC. He signed the result in 1529.

The panel is only 158 cm high and 120 cm wide (about 62 by 47 inches), smaller than many doors. Onto it Altdorfer packed thousands of soldiers, each with armor, a weapon and often a plume, some no bigger than a grain of rice.

The hanging tablet in the sky states the result in Latin, like a caption: Alexander defeats Darius, 100,000 Persian foot soldiers and more than 10,000 horsemen are killed, and the king's mother, wife and children are captured. So the two kings must be down there somewhere in the swarm.
Darius is fleeing in a chariot pulled by three white horses. Search the thick of the fight, left of center.

spots.title: Darius in flight
spots.text: Three white horses gallop to the left, dragging a golden chariot. The figure standing in it twists around to look back over his shoulder. The king of Persia is running, and he knows who is behind him.

lesson.text: Follow his backward glance to the right and you meet a rider in gold on a pale horse, a very long lance leveled at the chariot: Alexander. In a crowd this dense, how is anyone supposed to find him? Altdorfer built a set of signposts into the picture.
Three lines that turn a swarm into a story.

lines.label: The plumb line
lines.text: A cord with a red tassel and a ring hangs from the tablet. Keep dropping straight down from the ring, through the sea and the hills, and you arrive on Alexander. The caption points at its hero.

lines.label: The chase
lines.text: Alexander's lance aims left, straight at the chariot. Around this short line both armies bend like iron filings around a magnet, the Persians streaming away, the Greeks pouring after them.

lines.label: Sun to moon
lines.text: Above the armies a second line crosses the sky, from the sun going down on the right to a thin crescent moon in the top left corner. Day is ending as the battle is decided.

lesson.text: That sun and that moon are more than weather. The sun burns on Alexander's side of the world. The crescent hangs over the side of the fleeing Persians, and the crescent, for anyone alive in 1529, was the sign of the Ottoman Turks. The sky is taking sides.
Altdorfer's great invention was to make the landscape do the storytelling. The clouds whirl, the light splits, the earth itself seems to turn because two men are fighting on it.

The armies are not ancient either. Alexander's men wear the steel plate armor of German knights, and many of Darius's soldiers wear turbans. Altdorfer painted a battle from 1,800 years earlier as if it were the news. In a way it was.

In the autumn of 1529, the year on this painting, an Ottoman army laid siege to Vienna, a little over 300 km (about 200 miles) down the Danube from Regensburg. Altdorfer, as city architect, was put in charge of strengthening his own town's walls.

Then lift your eyes from the fight, and the picture does something no painting had done on this scale. The ground keeps going. Past the tents, past a city, the view climbs until you are looking down on seas and continents, as if from a mountain no one could ever climb.

lesson.title: The world above the battle
lesson.text: The upper half is a map painted as weather. Travel through it from the ground up.

spots.title: The camp
spots.text: Rows of pale tents ringed by a dark red barrier: the Persian camp, with columns of troops still marching out of it. Behind it rise the spires of a city that looks much more German than Asian.

spots.title: An island in the sea
spots.text: The dark island in the blue water is usually read as Cyprus. Beyond it the land narrows and more water opens up: the Red Sea, with the Nile nearby. Altdorfer is showing the whole eastern Mediterranean at once.

spots.title: The sun
spots.text: An orange disk sinks behind the mountains and sets the clouds spinning around it like water around a drain. Its glare runs across the sea toward us in a bright path.

spots.title: The moon
spots.text: A thin crescent in the darkest corner, with its own faint ring of clouds. It is as far from the sun as the panel allows.

lesson.text: This love of wild scenery was Altdorfer's signature. He belonged to a loose group of painters along the Danube who gave forests, peaks and skies the leading role, and he made some of the first European paintings with no people in them at all, pure landscapes. Here the two interests collide: a history lesson held inside a storm.

The panel has not come down to us untouched. At some point it was trimmed on every side, so the sky was once even larger, and the words on the tablet, first written in German, were repainted in Latin.

In 1800 French troops carried the painting off to Paris. Napoleon, who admired Alexander above all other generals, liked it so much that he hung it in his bathroom at the palace of Saint-Cloud. Prussian soldiers found it there in 1814, and it went home to Bavaria.

quiz.question: What did Altdorfer turn down in order to finish this painting?
options: The office of mayor of Regensburg
quiz.explanation: In 1528 his fellow councilors offered him the post of mayor and he refused.

quiz.question: How can you spot Darius in the crowd?
options: He stands alone on a hill
He flees in a chariot pulled by three white horses
quiz.explanation: The Persian king looks back from a golden chariot drawn by three white horses.

quiz.question: What hangs directly above Alexander, far up in the sky?
options: The cord and ring of the tablet
quiz.explanation: A line dropped from the tablet's ring lands on Alexander.

quiz.question: Why would the crescent moon have meant something special in 1529?
options: It was the Duke of Bavaria's emblem
It was the sign of the Ottoman Turks, who besieged Vienna that year
It marked the date of Easter
quiz.explanation: Viewers linked the crescent to the Ottomans, then advancing up the Danube.

quiz.question: What is unusual about the soldiers' equipment?
options: They wear armor and turbans of the painter's own time
They are all dressed as Romans
quiz.explanation: Altdorfer dressed an ancient battle in 16th-century plate armor and turbans.

facts.text: The painting is a wall-sized canvas more than five meters wide.
facts.explanation: It is a panel only about 158 by 120 cm.

facts.text: Napoleon hung the painting in his bathroom.
facts.explanation: After French troops took it in 1800, it hung in his bathroom at Saint-Cloud.

facts.text: The sun in the painting stands on the side of the fleeing Persians.
facts.explanation: The sun is on Alexander's side; the crescent moon hangs over the Persians.
